drill: Before writing code for a new feature or change, decide its name in the project's words, what callers can rely on, where it belongs, and the smallest write that delivers it. Use when the user asks to add, build, implement, or wire up something, or asks where it should live or what to call it, even when the change looks small enough to start coding at once. Do not use for a multi-stage migration that needs a staged plan with rollback.
dissect: Trace one code path to closure, proving every entry, caller, branch, state change, and effect. Use when the user asks who calls this, what reaches or touches it, how it flows, whether it is dead code, or to figure out what is really happening in some code, even when a quick search seems to answer it. Do not use to check claims or assumptions, or to map a whole area.
bulletproof: Surface the assumptions and claims a piece of work rests on and verify each against direct evidence. Use when the user asks are you sure, did you check, double-check this, or prove it, or before a statement, citation, plan, or done claim is relied on, even when you believe it is already right. Do not use to trace how code flows or for broad risk review.
revolver: Review code, diffs, plans, or documents through a sequential rotation of fresh reviewers, one risk stance at a time, resolving every finding before the next reviewer. Use when the user asks to review this top to bottom, for an adversarial, skeptical, or thorough review, or to tear it apart, even when the diff is small or pasted inline. Do not use to check a single claim.
panel: Recommend one option after independent analyses of real alternatives. Use when the user asks which option to pick, X or Y, or what you recommend between approaches for a consequential technical, product, or operational choice that evidence alone cannot decide, even when one option looks obvious. Do not use when evidence already decides it or the user has stated a decision.
